newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania PM says Italy-led force badly needed.
newsitem.headline: Albania PM says Italy-led force badly needed.

text.p: Albania's Prime Minister Bashkim Fino said on Wednesday the government can focus its efforts on fighting organised crime in the violence-plagued Balkan state once a multinational security force arrives.

In an interview with Reuters, Fino said the Italian-led security force due next week was needed to secure Albania's main ports and airport while giving the emergency all-party government time to reorganise its decimated security forces.

"The presence of these forces is very important for us because, in this difficult situation, our police are reorganising," Fino said. "Our police will thus have the chance to better focus on fighting against organised crime."

Fino, whose car was ambushed by armed bandits north of Tirana last week, said there were still considerable dangers lurking and vowed that his emergency all-party government would press forward with plans to hold elections within a few months.
"Anything might occur in Albania where many people are armed," he said when asked about the armed ambush.
Albania plunged into near-chaos when get-rich-quick schemes collapsed and armed rebels took control of the south during an unchecked spasm of looting and banditry.

More than 200 people have been killed and about 700 injured during the the violence that has swept the country, which was already Europe's poorest state. Army weapons depots were looted after soldiers and police abandoned their posts.
A strictly enforced 8 p.m. to 7 a.m. curfew has restored a semblance of order to the capital and surrounding area, but many regions are still viewed as effectively lawless.
About 6,000 troops from Italy, France, Spain, Turkey, Greece and Romania are expected to arrive starting April 14. They will protect the delivery of emergency food and medical supplies.

The 34-year-old prime minister, a leader of the leftist Socialist party, told Reuters he had no plans to respond to sharp criticism from President Sali Berisha, the embattled rightist who used unusually blunt language to blame Fino's Socialists for the mayhem.
"He can speak with this tongue," Fino said evenly after appearing surprised by Berisha's comments as they were read.

"Currently we don't intend to speak with the same language because we want to convey the message of peace, understanding and reconciliation to our people. The softer one speaks, the more the ballot boxes will be filled with free votes."
Berisha was quoted on Wednesday in an interview in the Austrian weekly magazine News as saying:

"The Socialists have pushed us into this situation. They spread hatred, acted like bandits, excluded themselves from political life in Albania. Their style created the climate of intolerance that has now led to the explosion."

Fino, whose Socialist party joined Berisha in an all-party emergency government on March 9, said in the interview in his tightly-guarded office it would not help Albania to criticise Berisha either now or during a forthcoming campaign ahead of early elections due in late June.

"This is not because we do not have sufficient motives to criticise his regime of the last five years," Fino said. "But we must abide by the political agreement of March 9, through which our government has got a much better message than (the previous one). I think that even during the electoral campaign we don't have to use that kind of language."
Berisha came to power in 1992. A former cardiologist, Berisha is blamed by many, especially in the south, for the collapse of the pyramid investment schemes.
Berisha appointed Fino, a Socialist, to lead the emergency 10-party government on March 12 and promised to hold early elections in June.
